Panorama in Decline

By: Carol Albertyn Christie | Commission

Proposal


Show:

Further information:
Title: Panorama in Decline: Who Let Our Tourist Treasures Rot?

Pitch Summary:
The Panorama Route in Mpumalanga boasts some of the most breathtaking scenery in South Africa — Bourke’s Luck Potholes, the Three Rondavels, God’s Window, and other world-class geological marvels. But behind the postcards lies a different reality: filthy ablutions, crumbling infrastructure, litter-strewn viewpoints, unsafe walkways, and a complete absence of onsite management.
The state of infrastructure along Mpumalanga’s Panorama Route has been laid bare in a 37-page report compiled by private-sector tourism stakeholders after a visit to several key government-managed tourist attractions earlier this month. The report – from Graskop Gorge Lift Company Co-Founder Oupa Pilane and Misty Mountain Owner Lisa Sheard – focuses on four sites managed by the Mpumalanga Tourism and Parks Agency (MTPA): Pinnacle Rock, God’s Window, Bourke’s Luck Potholes and Three Rondavels.
Using an adapted version of UN Tourism’s definition of “world-class” tourist attractions, the assessment covers criteria such as accessibility, cleanliness, general maintenance, health and safety compliance, staffing, tourist information, value-adds and community opportunities. Pilane and Sheard found the various criteria at all four sites to be between “substandard” and “unacceptably poor.”
The report states: “The prolonged neglect of maintenance and lack of investment in these four Panorama Route sites represents a significant and extended period of missed opportunity for economic growth, tourism growth and job creation in Mpumalanga.”
Despite charging entry fees, the sites fail to meet even basic standards of cleanliness, accessibility, and safety. The findings paint a picture of mismanagement and missed opportunity: world-class natural wonders reduced to “tired, old, dirty, messy, broken, neglected” attractions.
The report, the first in a series to be released in the coming weeks, will be presented to Mpumalanga MEC for Economic Development and Tourism Jesta Sidell with the ultimate aim to develop a regeneration plan for the Panorama Route.
Oupa Pilane comes to this not as a critic, but as a stakeholder. The Graskop Gorge Lift is Oupa Pilane’s flagship success — a world-class attraction that has redefined what tourism on the Panorama Route can be. Opened in 2018, it draws over 500,000 visitors a year, making it one of Mpumalanga’s biggest tourism successes. The site features Africa’s first viewing lift, carrying visitors 51 metres down the sheer cliff face into the lush Afromontane forest below. Guests can explore a 600-metre circular trail with interactive exhibits, cross a suspension bridge linking both sides of the gorge, and experience adrenaline attractions like the Big Swing and ziplines. On site are two restaurants, a community craft market, retail outlets, and viewing decks with sweeping views of the gorge and waterfall. Pilane’s model — combining natural beauty, innovation, community involvement, and sound management — shows exactly what is possible when vision meets execution.
Situated close to the Kruger National Park and running along the world’s third-largest canyon, the Blyde River Canyon, the Panorama Route has long been regarded as an attractive add-on to international tourist itineraries. But operators told Tourism Update this allure has started to wane.
“An international tourist comes from a five-star lodge and then arrives at these poorly maintained sites, filled with litter, understaffed and with buildings in a shocking state. It’s a very sad state of affairs,” said Jaco Scheepers, Owner of Hoedspruit-based Sable Tours.
Scheepers said he no longer takes clients to the historical gold mining village of Pilgrim’s Rest – once a thriving tourist site. “The town is overrun with illegal miners and many of the historical buildings have been stripped of their steel roofing and windows. We can no longer market it as an attractive choice.”
Tom Vorster, Acting Chair of the Maruleng Tourism Association, said he has witnessed a growing number of tour operators removing the Panorama Route from itineraries. “From a personal perspective, when recommending the Panorama Route to visitors, I often suggest they skip the MTPA sites and head directly to Graskop Gorge, which offers stunning views, engaging attractions and well-maintained facilities,” said Vorster.
The MTPA previously told Tourism Update that infrastructure maintenance has been challenged by budgetary constraints but asserted that the agency was “immediately focusing on fixing some of those amenities to return to their normal functionality and appearance.”
Key Angles / Questions:
• How much revenue do these attractions generate annually, and where does it go?
• Why have basic health and safety issues — broken railings, unsafe ablutions — gone unaddressed for years?
• Why is there no effective onsite management at flagship tourist destinations?
• How does this neglect affect local job creation and tourism potential?
• Are there successful public-private tourism management models elsewhere in SA that could be replicated here?
• Should private sector partnerships be the solution to rescuing these attractions?
Potential Interviewees:
1. Oupa Pilane – Tourism and Graskop Gorge Lift (0823718413, oupa@gglc.co.za)
2. Lisa Sheard – Misty Mountain Owner (0832479732, lisa@mistymountain.co.za)
3. Gavin – Tour operator
4. Craft operators at venues
5. Mpumalanga Tourism and Parks Agency – Chairperson: Mr Victor Mashego (info@mtpa.co.za, +27 (0)13 065 0859)
Visual Elements:
• Striking aerial footage of the natural wonders (Bourke’s Luck Potholes, Three Rondavels, God’s Window)
• Close-ups of neglect: litter, broken infrastructure, dirty ablutions, crumbling railings, and unsafe walkways
• Contrasts with promotional tourism material claiming “world-class” standards
• Interviews on location with tourists expressing shock and disappointment
• Comparative footage of well-managed sites elsewhere in SA or abroad
Why Now:
Tourism is a critical sector for South Africa’s economy, and international arrivals are recovering post-COVID. Neglecting world-class sites risks reputational damage just as the country needs to attract visitors. With the rand weak, SA is well-positioned to be a competitive travel destination — but only if it delivers on its promise. This story raises urgent questions of accountability, governance, and the future of our tourism treasures.
MTPA: Leadership, Mandate & Budget
• Chairperson: Victor Mashego
• CEO: Mduduzi Vilakazi
• Acting CFO: Fikile Ngobeni
Annual Budget
• ~R514 million (2023–24)
• ~R512 million (2024–25)
Purpose
• Conservation of parks and promotion of tourism across Mpumalanga
Recent Concerns
• Claims of poor maintenance, inefficiency raised in July 2025
Mandate:
• Conserve and manage public nature reserves and wilderness areas across Mpumalanga (e.g., Blyde River Canyon, Barberton Nature Reserve, Verloren Valei)
• Promote tourism through infrastructure, site maintenance, marketing, and support services
Experiential Travel: Context for the Crisis
People want more from vacations — not just a beautiful beach. They want meaning, connection, and shareable experiences. Called experiential travel or immersion travel, this style of tourism focuses on meaningful, immersive experiences that connect travellers with the culture, people, environment, or activities of a destination. Rather than simply sightseeing, experiential travellers seek to participate—whether that’s learning to cook with locals, volunteering on conservation projects, or hiking lesser-known routes with community guides. The aim is engagement over observation, and authenticity over convenience.
Why It’s Increased Post-Pandemic:
1. Shift in values – After the isolation and uncertainty of the COVID-19 pandemic, many travellers now prioritise connection, purpose, and presence. Mass tourism feels hollow; meaningful interaction feels urgent.
2. Desire for slower travel – Lockdowns forced a slower pace of life. Post-pandemic, travellers seek deeper engagement over fast itineraries and crowded tourist hubs.
3. Support for local economies – With international tourism collapsing during COVID, travellers are more aware of their spending power. Experiential travel often directly benefits small businesses, artisans, and communities.
4. Mental health and wellness – Experiences that offer emotional connection, personal growth, or physical activity (like nature retreats or cultural exchanges) are increasingly valued as a counterweight to stress and burnout.
5. Digital fatigue – In an age of remote work and screen overload, travellers crave tactile, real-world experiences that can't be replicated online.
Despite a 15.6% year-on-year increase in international tourist arrivals to 2.1 million in 2024, visitor spend remains “low due to limited or outdated tourism product offerings”, according to MEC Jesta Sidell.
If I own a house and something goes wrong, I fix it. I do it to keep the value of my property. If this were my house, I would have repainted the railing, fixed the toilet. There is no big thinking of how to make this viewing spot unique. It’s an outdated tourist model.

Panorama Script FINAL

(Pilot) It produces water for the Lowveld, so it’s such valuable conservation area.
(Claire) It’s sunset. We’re flying over the Blyde River Canyon — the heart of Mpumalanga’s Panorama Route.
(PILOT) This is the world’s largest green canyon.
(Claire) Green canyon. Yes.
(Claire) Below, the Drakensberg escarpment with iconic sights — the Three Rondavels, Bourke’s Luck Potholes and God’s Window.
From afar, awe inspiring.
(Claire) Okay. ( Laughs and screams)
(Claire) But up close… A damning report warns these treasures are being left to rot.
(OUPA) Everything there is falling apart. There's litter everywhere.
(LISA ) Fences are falling down. Railings look unsafe.
(SANDILE) Sometimes no water, so everything it’s not looking good.
(Claire) Despite a budget of more than R500 million… at some sites, tourists have washed their hands from a two-litre bottle and a bucket.
(OUPA) I mean, how low can we really stoop for us to reach that level where we can't even have working toilets? And yet these tourists are paying money to come in.
(Claire) Mpumalanga means the place where the sun rises. Millions come each year, not just for the Kruger Park, but for these escarpment wonders.
(OUPA) We’ve got the most amazing province. It’s like when God created heaven and earth he just said, let there be Mpumalanga.
(Claire) Oupa Pilane is a tourism entrepreneur and partner in the Graskop Gorge Lift Company — the Panorama Route’s flagship attraction.

(Oupa) We are a nature based adventure centre. So what we wanted to do, was to integrate this beautiful afromountain forest with adventure activities. So that you can then allow people to have multiple experiences.
(Claire) There’s something for everyone here — bungee jumping, zip-lining, or a quiet meditation at the rock pool. Experiential tourism that works: more than 1.3 million visitors in just seven years.
(Claire) Today, I’m strapping in for their latest test of nerves… a 60-metre descent on a sliver of wood.
(Claire) The trust I have in this cable.
(Claire) Laughs.

(Claire) Many Carte Blanche stories take us to the cliff’s edge. And today, I’m literally on the edge.
But what’s more worrying is that Mpumalanga’s iconic Panorama Route has fallen off a cliff of a different kind.

(Claire) Lisa Sheard has spent a lifetime in tourism, and is concerned that there may be no climbing back.
(Lisa) They're failing because the infrastructure's crumbled. Where the infrastructure is poor, it’s neglected, the place is dirty, things don't work. There's no sense of pride in those places. So when you arrive as a tourist, you get a terrible sinking feeling because you just get the feeling that it is neglected and nobody cares.

(OUPA) And when you have a travel agent that brings over a thousand visitors to this site says, I've decided not to come there anymore, because I really don't have value for money and my clients complain. That becomes a cause for concern.

(Claire) These sites are managed by the Mpumalanga Tourism and Parks Agency, or MTPA. After years of begging for better maintenance, Oupa and Lisa invited the agency to visit the Panorama Route and see the decay of their sites first-hand. The MTPA declined — suggesting a boardroom meeting instead.

(Oupa) There is no point in us meeting in boardrooms in Nelspruit, because the problem is here. You can simple see the neglect on this site.
(Claire) Frustrated by the lack of vision and accountability, Oupa and Lisa took to the road with the media to show them the state of the sites: Pinnacle Rock, God’s Window, Bourke’s Luck Potholes, and the three Rondavels. They released a report with photographic evidence.
(Oupa) We cannot continue to be like this. This place has got one of the most highest unemployment. And yet we are sitting with these jewels. Jewels that can create over 2000 jobs, if we focus on the Panorama and creating amazing attractions.
(Claire) The report went viral – and finally, the MPTA was forced to listen. But Acting CEO Justus Mohlala said in a radio interview, that he was “perplexed” by the findings.
(Justus) I am not aware of any challenges. We are doing well, we have done well in the past 6 years in terms of our international tourist arrivals, as well as the tourism trips on the domestic market.
(Claire) To assess the lay of the land, we’re going on our own Panorama Route pilgrimage and giving each stop a score of its own. First up: God’s Window.
(Claire) They call this God’s Window and on a clear day you can see why. The spectacular views of the Lowveld are absolutely breathtaking. But unfortunately if you look a little closer you see rusted railings, litter on the floor and dilapidated infrastructure.

(Claire) A hard push on this rusted railing could send a tourist over the edge. The decay is everywhere: a payment board propped up with a stone, broken basins, cracked windows. No greeting. No map. No information.
For independent tour guide Sandile Mokoena, who brings overseas visitors here, it’s a constant frustration.
(Claire) How do you deal with those situations when there is no water and the toilets aren’t working?
(Sandile) So, most of the time, this site we make sure that we come early as possible, because the last stop will be Graskop Gorge where I know that everything is sorted.
(Claire) Is it sometimes embarrassing to be showing people these things and they are not working?
(Sandile) It is embarrassing. Cause remember those people are coming from outside and they are paying a lot of money, what do they do with the money? Because they were supposed to fix everything that needs to be fixed inside here, but they don’t.
(Claire) The MTPA gets more than R500 million a year from national government to manage reserves and sites. Salaries swallow the grant. But these sites draw hundreds of thousands of tourists a year – all paying entry fees.
(Claire) Generating. Do we understand how much revenue?
(LISA) So you're looking at about 42 million rand that they generate from gate entry and from the concessions. Of which, last year, in their annual financial statements, they spent 3 million on infrastructural maintenance on all MPTA properties. So that's all of them.
(Claire) It’s no surprise the sites look the way they do. At God’s Window, Oupa and Lisa’s report seems to have jolted the MTPA into action — at least on the surface. The toilets flush, the grass is trimmed. The view is world-class. The facilities — anything but. Our score: D.
(Claire) We head north…
(Claire) Over thousands of years, swirling waters drill cylindrical pools into solid rock. They’re called Bourke’s Luck Potholes named after a prospector who never struck gold but whose name endures in one of South Africa’s natural wonders.
(Claire) The report has had its impact here too. The site is tidy, the toilets are working. But the rails are unpainted and the signage damaged.
Our assessment: priceless natural heritage gets second-rate support. On our scorecard: a C.
(Claire) Everyone agrees the quick fixes are new, but the neglect is not. So, we go to Mpumalanga Tourism for answers.
(Claire) Acting CEO Justus Mohlala’s predecessor, Mduduzi Vilakazi, was suspended last year on charges of maladministration and corruption. By the time he sits down with us, Mohlala, too, is being replaced.
(Claire) What is your assessment of the Panorama routes?
(Justus) Since we, we got to know about this problem. We have been having a team on site to make sure that ablution facilities are functional.
(Claire) Since his radio interview, Mohlala has changed his tune. But he’s apparently unconcerned by the possibility that poor facilities might deter tourists.

(Justus) What I need to indicate, you still receive the natural splendour of the Panorama Route. It's more about nature. The waterfalls are still dropping down. The experience of the potholes, the water meandering inside the rocks. It's still happening. So we want to acknowledge that it’s something that has been troubling us due to budget constraints.
(Claire) The budget constraints don’t seem to apply to the ablutions at Head office.
(Oupa) MTPA has contracted a private company to provide them with clean toilets in their head office. But their toilets are spick and span. And yet the sites where people are paying, we've got no working toilets.
(Claire) Now to our last stop — the Three Rondavels, amongst the most photographed landmarks on the Panorama Route.
(Claire) Here too, the site has been tidied and the toilets are working. But the same tell-tale signs of neglect are evident.
(Claire) On our scorecard: another wasted chance… just D+.

(Claire) Our tour has put Graskop in sharp perspective: this is what’s possible when those in charge of a site are invested in its success. It’s the polar opposite of the apathy that lingers over the state-managed sites we’ve seen.
(Claire) When I first visited Graskop over 25 years ago, nothing was here. And to see what they have managed to build in that time is actually mind blowing. Now imagine if that vision and investment was put back into the Panorama Route. Imagine how many more visitors would be visiting this iconic area.

(Claire) The pressure appears to have paid off. Mpumalanga Tourism has promised to ring-fence gate takings for maintenance and upgrades. And the agency says it is more open to developing the Panorama sites the way Graskop has been transformed.

(OUPA) South Africa needs more people that are speaking out. If we are to save our country, if we are to create employment, if we are to grow the economy of this country. We need people to speak out.
(Claire)
Back on the cliff walk… it takes nerves of steel. A fitting place to end — on the edge. Because so is the Panorama Route.
(Claire) Screams.

Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 21 September 2025 TX Date: 0000-00-00 Script: Panorama Script FINAL (Pilot) It produces water for the Lowveld, so it’s such valuable conservation area. (Claire) It’s sunset. We’re flying over the Blyde River Canyon — the heart of Mpumalanga’s Panorama Route. (PILOT) This is the world’s largest green canyon. (Claire) Green canyon. Yes. (Claire) Below, the Drakensberg escarpment with iconic sights — the Three Rondavels, Bourke’s Luck Potholes and God’s Window. From afar, awe inspiring. (Claire) Okay. ( Laughs and screams) (Claire) But up close… A damning report warns these treasures are being left to rot. (OUPA) Everything there is falling apart. There's litter everywhere. (LISA ) Fences are falling down. Railings look unsafe. (SANDILE) Sometimes no water, so everything it’s not looking good. (Claire) Despite a budget of more than R500 million… at some sites, tourists have washed their hands from a two-litre bottle and a bucket. (OUPA) I mean, how low can we really stoop for us to reach that level where we can't even have working toilets? And yet these tourists are paying money to come in. (Claire) Mpumalanga means the place where the sun rises. Millions come each year, not just for the Kruger Park, but for these escarpment wonders. (OUPA) We’ve got the most amazing province. It’s like when God created heaven and earth he just said, let there be Mpumalanga. (Claire) Oupa Pilane is a tourism entrepreneur and partner in the Graskop Gorge Lift Company — the Panorama Route’s flagship attraction. (Oupa) We are a nature based adventure centre. So what we wanted to do, was to integrate this beautiful afromountain forest with adventure activities. So that you can then allow people to have multiple experiences. (Claire) There’s something for everyone here — bungee jumping, zip-lining, or a quiet meditation at the rock pool. Experiential tourism that works: more than 1.3 million visitors in just seven years. (Claire) Today, I’m strapping in for their latest test of nerves… a 60-metre descent on a sliver of wood. (Claire) The trust I have in this cable. (Claire) Laughs. (Claire) Many Carte Blanche stories take us to the cliff’s edge. And today, I’m literally on the edge. But what’s more worrying is that Mpumalanga’s iconic Panorama Route has fallen off a cliff of a different kind. (Claire) Lisa Sheard has spent a lifetime in tourism, and is concerned that there may be no climbing back. (Lisa) They're failing because the infrastructure's crumbled. Where the infrastructure is poor, it’s neglected, the place is dirty, things don't work. There's no sense of pride in those places. So when you arrive as a tourist, you get a terrible sinking feeling because you just get the feeling that it is neglected and nobody cares. (OUPA) And when you have a travel agent that brings over a thousand visitors to this site says, I've decided not to come there anymore, because I really don't have value for money and my clients complain. That becomes a cause for concern. (Claire) These sites are managed by the Mpumalanga Tourism and Parks Agency, or MTPA. After years of begging for better maintenance, Oupa and Lisa invited the agency to visit the Panorama Route and see the decay of their sites first-hand. The MTPA declined — suggesting a boardroom meeting instead. (Oupa) There is no point in us meeting in boardrooms in Nelspruit, because the problem is here. You can simple see the neglect on this site. (Claire) Frustrated by the lack of vision and accountability, Oupa and Lisa took to the road with the media to show them the state of the sites: Pinnacle Rock, God’s Window, Bourke’s Luck Potholes, and the three Rondavels. They released a report with photographic evidence. (Oupa) We cannot continue to be like this. This place has got one of the most highest unemployment. And yet we are sitting with these jewels. Jewels that can create over 2000 jobs, if we focus on the Panorama and creating amazing attractions. (Claire) The report went viral – and finally, the MPTA was forced to listen. But Acting CEO Justus Mohlala said in a radio interview, that he was “perplexed” by the findings. (Justus) I am not aware of any challenges. We are doing well, we have done well in the past 6 years in terms of our international tourist arrivals, as well as the tourism trips on the domestic market. (Claire) To assess the lay of the land, we’re going on our own Panorama Route pilgrimage and giving each stop a score of its own. First up: God’s Window. (Claire) They call this God’s Window and on a clear day you can see why. The spectacular views of the Lowveld are absolutely breathtaking. But unfortunately if you look a little closer you see rusted railings, litter on the floor and dilapidated infrastructure. (Claire) A hard push on this rusted railing could send a tourist over the edge. The decay is everywhere: a payment board propped up with a stone, broken basins, cracked windows. No greeting. No map. No information. For independent tour guide Sandile Mokoena, who brings overseas visitors here, it’s a constant frustration. (Claire) How do you deal with those situations when there is no water and the toilets aren’t working? (Sandile) So, most of the time, this site we make sure that we come early as possible, because the last stop will be Graskop Gorge where I know that everything is sorted. (Claire) Is it sometimes embarrassing to be showing people these things and they are not working? (Sandile) It is embarrassing. Cause remember those people are coming from outside and they are paying a lot of money, what do they do with the money? Because they were supposed to fix everything that needs to be fixed inside here, but they don’t. (Claire) The MTPA gets more than R500 million a year from national government to manage reserves and sites. Salaries swallow the grant. But these sites draw hundreds of thousands of tourists a year – all paying entry fees. (Claire) Generating. Do we understand how much revenue? (LISA) So you're looking at about 42 million rand that they generate from gate entry and from the concessions. Of which, last year, in their annual financial statements, they spent 3 million on infrastructural maintenance on all MPTA properties. So that's all of them. (Claire) It’s no surprise the sites look the way they do. At God’s Window, Oupa and Lisa’s report seems to have jolted the MTPA into action — at least on the surface. The toilets flush, the grass is trimmed. The view is world-class. The facilities — anything but. Our score: D. (Claire) We head north… (Claire) Over thousands of years, swirling waters drill cylindrical pools into solid rock. They’re called Bourke’s Luck Potholes named after a prospector who never struck gold but whose name endures in one of South Africa’s natural wonders. (Claire) The report has had its impact here too. The site is tidy, the toilets are working. But the rails are unpainted and the signage damaged. Our assessment: priceless natural heritage gets second-rate support. On our scorecard: a C. (Claire) Everyone agrees the quick fixes are new, but the neglect is not. So, we go to Mpumalanga Tourism for answers. (Claire) Acting CEO Justus Mohlala’s predecessor, Mduduzi Vilakazi, was suspended last year on charges of maladministration and corruption. By the time he sits down with us, Mohlala, too, is being replaced. (Claire) What is your assessment of the Panorama routes? (Justus) Since we, we got to know about this problem. We have been having a team on site to make sure that ablution facilities are functional. (Claire) Since his radio interview, Mohlala has changed his tune. But he’s apparently unconcerned by the possibility that poor facilities might deter tourists. (Justus) What I need to indicate, you still receive the natural splendour of the Panorama Route. It's more about nature. The waterfalls are still dropping down. The experience of the potholes, the water meandering inside the rocks. It's still happening. So we want to acknowledge that it’s something that has been troubling us due to budget constraints. (Claire) The budget constraints don’t seem to apply to the ablutions at Head office. (Oupa) MTPA has contracted a private company to provide them with clean toilets in their head office. But their toilets are spick and span. And yet the sites where people are paying, we've got no working toilets. (Claire) Now to our last stop — the Three Rondavels, amongst the most photographed landmarks on the Panorama Route. (Claire) Here too, the site has been tidied and the toilets are working. But the same tell-tale signs of neglect are evident. (Claire) On our scorecard: another wasted chance… just D+. (Claire) Our tour has put Graskop in sharp perspective: this is what’s possible when those in charge of a site are invested in its success. It’s the polar opposite of the apathy that lingers over the state-managed sites we’ve seen. (Claire) When I first visited Graskop over 25 years ago, nothing was here. And to see what they have managed to build in that time is actually mind blowing. Now imagine if that vision and investment was put back into the Panorama Route. Imagine how many more visitors would be visiting this iconic area. (Claire) The pressure appears to have paid off. Mpumalanga Tourism has promised to ring-fence gate takings for maintenance and upgrades. And the agency says it is more open to developing the Panorama sites the way Graskop has been transformed. (OUPA) South Africa needs more people that are speaking out. If we are to save our country, if we are to create employment, if we are to grow the economy of this country. We need people to speak out. (Claire) Back on the cliff walk… it takes nerves of steel. A fitting place to end — on the edge. Because so is the Panorama Route. (Claire) Screams.

metadata.Further information: Title: Panorama in Decline: Who Let Our Tourist Treasures Rot? Pitch Summary: The Panorama Route in Mpumalanga boasts some of the most breathtaking scenery in South Africa — Bourke’s Luck Potholes, the Three Rondavels, God’s Window, and other world-class geological marvels. But behind the postcards lies a different reality: filthy ablutions, crumbling infrastructure, litter-strewn viewpoints, unsafe walkways, and a complete absence of onsite management. The state of infrastructure along Mpumalanga’s Panorama Route has been laid bare in a 37-page report compiled by private-sector tourism stakeholders after a visit to several key government-managed tourist attractions earlier this month. The report – from Graskop Gorge Lift Company Co-Founder Oupa Pilane and Misty Mountain Owner Lisa Sheard – focuses on four sites managed by the Mpumalanga Tourism and Parks Agency (MTPA): Pinnacle Rock, God’s Window, Bourke’s Luck Potholes and Three Rondavels. Using an adapted version of UN Tourism’s definition of “world-class” tourist attractions, the assessment covers criteria such as accessibility, cleanliness, general maintenance, health and safety compliance, staffing, tourist information, value-adds and community opportunities. Pilane and Sheard found the various criteria at all four sites to be between “substandard” and “unacceptably poor.” The report states: “The prolonged neglect of maintenance and lack of investment in these four Panorama Route sites represents a significant and extended period of missed opportunity for economic growth, tourism growth and job creation in Mpumalanga.” Despite charging entry fees, the sites fail to meet even basic standards of cleanliness, accessibility, and safety. The findings paint a picture of mismanagement and missed opportunity: world-class natural wonders reduced to “tired, old, dirty, messy, broken, neglected” attractions. The report, the first in a series to be released in the coming weeks, will be presented to Mpumalanga MEC for Economic Development and Tourism Jesta Sidell with the ultimate aim to develop a regeneration plan for the Panorama Route. Oupa Pilane comes to this not as a critic, but as a stakeholder. The Graskop Gorge Lift is Oupa Pilane’s flagship success — a world-class attraction that has redefined what tourism on the Panorama Route can be. Opened in 2018, it draws over 500,000 visitors a year, making it one of Mpumalanga’s biggest tourism successes. The site features Africa’s first viewing lift, carrying visitors 51 metres down the sheer cliff face into the lush Afromontane forest below. Guests can explore a 600-metre circular trail with interactive exhibits, cross a suspension bridge linking both sides of the gorge, and experience adrenaline attractions like the Big Swing and ziplines. On site are two restaurants, a community craft market, retail outlets, and viewing decks with sweeping views of the gorge and waterfall. Pilane’s model — combining natural beauty, innovation, community involvement, and sound management — shows exactly what is possible when vision meets execution. Situated close to the Kruger National Park and running along the world’s third-largest canyon, the Blyde River Canyon, the Panorama Route has long been regarded as an attractive add-on to international tourist itineraries. But operators told Tourism Update this allure has started to wane. “An international tourist comes from a five-star lodge and then arrives at these poorly maintained sites, filled with litter, understaffed and with buildings in a shocking state. It’s a very sad state of affairs,” said Jaco Scheepers, Owner of Hoedspruit-based Sable Tours. Scheepers said he no longer takes clients to the historical gold mining village of Pilgrim’s Rest – once a thriving tourist site. “The town is overrun with illegal miners and many of the historical buildings have been stripped of their steel roofing and windows. We can no longer market it as an attractive choice.” Tom Vorster, Acting Chair of the Maruleng Tourism Association, said he has witnessed a growing number of tour operators removing the Panorama Route from itineraries. “From a personal perspective, when recommending the Panorama Route to visitors, I often suggest they skip the MTPA sites and head directly to Graskop Gorge, which offers stunning views, engaging attractions and well-maintained facilities,” said Vorster. The MTPA previously told Tourism Update that infrastructure maintenance has been challenged by budgetary constraints but asserted that the agency was “immediately focusing on fixing some of those amenities to return to their normal functionality and appearance.” Key Angles / Questions: • How much revenue do these attractions generate annually, and where does it go? • Why have basic health and safety issues — broken railings, unsafe ablutions — gone unaddressed for years? • Why is there no effective onsite management at flagship tourist destinations? • How does this neglect affect local job creation and tourism potential? • Are there successful public-private tourism management models elsewhere in SA that could be replicated here? • Should private sector partnerships be the solution to rescuing these attractions?
